trajectory_summary: The call opens cold and confused, briefly stabilizes into normal verify-script rhythm, then derails when the credit qualifier triggers an elder-fraud disclosure the rep never engages with. From that point the call becomes a one-sided loop: the customer escalates emotional detail, the rep repeats the same scripted line, and the call ends with no resolution and no next step.
outcome_dispute: If v1 tagged this as a standard callback, that undersells what happened — there is no scheduled or implied timeframe for the customer to 'get back' and no acknowledgment of the vulnerability that is the actual blocker. This is better read as an unresolved disqualification-in-limbo: the call ends on an unanchored instruction to check credit, not a real callback commitment from either party.

observed_outcome.quote: And so we just we would just need to make sure that it would be above $6.50 in order to help you out. And so just reach back out to us when it is. Okay? Have a great rest of your day. Bye bye.
observed_outcome.reasoning: The call ends with no appointment, no confirmed callback time, and no next step owned by the rep — only a passive instruction for the customer to reach back out once he determines his credit score, which is not a scheduled callback in any meaningful sense.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The call never reaches bill collection — it stalls at the credit qualifier following the fraud disclosure and ends shortly after without any bill amount or usage figure being discussed.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never asks what interested the customer in solar; the call moves from address/roof verification straight into the bill-swap program pitch and credit qualifier before stalling, so no interest reason was ever solicited or given.

primary_coaching_focus.quote: I'm 81 years old. These assholes are about 20, 30, 40 years old during the, COVID nineteen epidemic.
primary_coaching_focus.why: An 81-year-old customer disclosed elder fraud victimization and a hospitalization-related home invasion, and the rep's response across five separate touches never moved past a two-word acknowledgment before returning to the credit-score script line. This is the single most consequential miss on the call — it directly cost any chance at trust or a real next step, and it is a repeatable pattern the manager should watch for on other calls with this rep.

key_moments.quote: You say you have a design already?
key_moments.stewart_read: This is an early legitimacy probe — the customer is checking whether the rep is overstating what's actually been done for him, which lines up with his later disclosure of being a repeated fraud target. Read in isolation it looks like a stray misunderstanding; read against the 03:57 and 04:13 disclosures, it's the first sign of the same scam-vigilance that drives the rest of the call.

key_moments.quote: Okay. So has the roof not been replaced since?
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer had just asked the rep to clarify whether she meant the house or the shingles; the rep's next line re-asks a version of the same ambiguous question rather than acknowledging his clarification request. This is an attentiveness lapse, not a knowledge gap — the rep has the information, she's just not tracking the customer's back-and-forth.

key_moments.quote: Somebody somebody's been using my name to get stuff, in the past.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the first instance of a fraud/vulnerability disclosure. The rep's next line ('Alright. That's good.') is a scripted transition filler, not an acknowledgment of the disclosure's content — it treats emotionally loaded information as a scheduling checkbox.

key_moments.stewart_read: Customer discloses his age and a home invasion / hospitalization story in escalating detail. The rep's response, 'They did.', is a two-word acknowledgment with zero emotional content, immediately followed by a return to the script's credit threshold line.
